title: Questioning the problem-solving process
hook: Red pins on three late-night bus routes can tempt Megan to buy buses before she knows the problem.
counterintuition: Why does a sharp recommendation backfire? It can jump from symptom to fix before the problem and causes have been separated.
tryThisNow: Write three lines for one current issue: symptom, possible cause, and proposed action. If the first and third lines match, define the problem again.
keyTakeaway: Separate symptom, cause, and action before trusting a recommendation; structure the inquiry before the final hierarchy carries it.

breakdown.fastRead:
A wall map shows red pins along three late-night bus routes. Megan hears the easy fix: add buses. She writes late buses as a symptom, then splits the issue into dispatch gaps, traffic, and transfer timing. No service plan goes out until each branch is tested.

Problem solving needs its own order. What happened? Why? What should change? If those jobs blur, the final outline may look firm while carrying a shortcut inside it.
breakdown.deepRead:
Are patients rejecting the food, or is the food arriving too late to be food? Etienne asks in the hospital cafeteria office, with tray return counts beside a temperature log and dietary-order sheet. The team predicts taste is the problem and starts talking about a new menu.

Étienne builds branches first: delivery timing, tray temperature, dietary fit, menu choice. Only then can the team decide where action belongs.

A logic tree earns its keep only when it opens the field of causes before one favorite explanation takes over. It is not a decorative diagram. It is a way to prevent a symptom from hardening into a recommendation before diagnosis has happened.

Definition comes first. Diagnosis comes second. Action comes third.

The order protects the reader from borrowed certainty. If the problem is poorly named, every branch below it inherits the error. If diagnosis is skipped, action becomes a guess with a firm voice. If the field is never branched, one loud explanation can crowd out quieter causes.

This pause is not delay for its own sake. It is the moment when the team stops asking which answer sounds plausible and starts asking which branches the evidence can rule in or out. A thin problem statement makes every later choice look stronger than it is.
breakdown.fullRead:
A tray of cloudy wells sits under the lab hood light while Paula reconstructs a failed replication. The result is visible: the assay failed again. The temptation is also visible: retrain the technician or replace the reagent lot. Either fix may be right. Neither has earned its place yet.

Paula labels the failure as the visible result, not the problem statement. Then she builds a cause tree: technique, reagent quality, sample preparation, incubation timing. The replication log supports one branch. The reagent lot sheet supports another. The sample prep checklist exposes a third. Only after the branches exist can she choose whether retraining or replacement belongs in the action line.

Definition, diagnosis, and action are different jobs; when they blur, the outline starts carrying borrowed certainty. The heading map separates the questions for a reason: what is the problem, why does it exist, what should be done about it. Structure belongs inside the inquiry, not only inside the final report.

Try this with any issue that feels obvious. Write the symptom in one line. Write at least three possible cause branches. Write the action last. If the action is already present in the first line, you probably named your preferred fix as the problem.

Chris learns that in a bookshop. Sales are down is too blunt to guide action. After three quiet Tuesdays, he branches the issue into foot traffic, conversion, and basket size. The construction notice explains one branch, the category inventory report explains another, and the daily sales ledger tests the pattern. Discounting no longer looks like the first move.

Marit faces a more public version in a storm-shelter review. Slow shelter openings could be staffing, keys, alerts, or supplies. If she writes staff failed before checking the radio log and key-control sheet, she turns one possible cause into the official problem. She divides the process into alert, access, staffing, and supply branches, then marks which branch lacks evidence.

The limit is important. A logic tree can become busywork if it keeps dividing after the useful field is visible. The goal is not to draw every possible branch. The goal is to open enough of the field that the recommendation no longer outruns the diagnosis.

Akira uses the same discipline in a game studio. The build failure is on the screen, but it is not the problem yet. Assets, code merges, tests, and release timing all have to be separated before the team buys tooling or rewrites handoff rules. The final recommendation gains force because the process behind it has stopped bluffing.

A polished hierarchy cannot rescue a lazy inquiry. The structure on the page has to be backed by structure in the thinking that produced it.

A cause tree earns its keep when it opens the field of causes before one favorite explanation takes over. What is the problem / why does it exist / what should we do about it is not a slogan; it is a sequence that keeps definition, diagnosis, and action from blurring.

examples.title: Megan Branches the Late-Bus Problem

planSpec.domain: a public-transit planning unit investigating late evening buses
planSpec.stakes: the city may add buses when the real issue is dispatch gaps or transfer timing
planSpec.requiredBeat: Megan writes late buses as a symptom, branches the issue into dispatch, traffic, and transfer timing, and refuses to recommend added service until each branch is tested.

examples.scenario: Megan stands at the planning table as a wall map shows red pins along three late-night routes in the transit planning unit. Megan has the dispatch log open beside a transfer timing table, and the council aide wants a service recommendation by noon. She faces a choice: call late buses the problem and add vehicles, or treat lateness as a symptom. She branches the issue into dispatch, traffic, and transfer timing and refuses to recommend added service until each branch is tested.
examples.whatToDo: Define lateness as an observed result. Compare likely cause buckets against the log before any service fix is named.
examples.whyItMatters: The city may buy buses to solve a scheduling or transfer problem. Branching the issue keeps action from outrunning diagnosis.

examples.title: Etienne Branches the Meal Returns

planSpec.domain: a hospital cafeteria team analyzing uneaten patient meals
planSpec.stakes: budget will be spent on new menus if timing, temperature, or dietary mismatches are not separated
planSpec.requiredBeat: Étienne asks whether taste is the problem, then builds branches for delivery timing, tray temperature, dietary fit, and menu choice before recommending anything.

examples.scenario: Etienne asks whether patients are rejecting the food, or whether the food is arriving too late to be food as the hospital analyst beside tray return counts, a temperature log, and dietary-order sheets. The cafeteria team predicts taste is the problem and starts pricing menu work. Étienne must decide whether to endorse that fix or branch the causes first. He draws delivery timing, tray temperature, dietary fit, and menu choice before recommending anything.
examples.whatToDo: Build cause branches before spending menu money. Test timing, temperature, dietary fit, and menu choice as separate explanations.
examples.whyItMatters: Uneaten meals are a symptom. A new menu only helps if menu choice is the cause, not if temperature or timing is breaking the experience.

examples.title: Paula Builds the Cause Tree First

planSpec.domain: a university lab investigating failed replication attempts
planSpec.audience: research teams structuring inquiry before corrective action
planSpec.stakes: months of work may be wasted if technique, reagent quality, and sample preparation are not diagnosed separately
planSpec.requiredBeat: Paula labels the failure as the visible result, then builds a cause tree before choosing whether to retrain staff or replace reagents.

examples.scenario: Paula reviews a tray of cloudy wells under the lab hood light after the third failed replication and checks the replication log, reagent lot sheet, and sample prep checklist in the postmortem. The visible result is failure, but the corrective action is still open. She labels the cloudy wells as result, builds a cause tree for technique, reagent quality, and sample preparation, then chooses between retraining and replacement only after the branches have evidence.
examples.whatToDo: Treat the failed assay as the visible result. Build a cause tree before selecting retraining, reagent replacement, or sample-prep repair.
examples.whyItMatters: Research teams waste months when the first visible result becomes the problem. Diagnosis needs branches before action deserves confidence.

examples.title: Chris Stops Calling Sales the Problem

planSpec.domain: a bookshop owner tracing declining weekday sales
planSpec.stakes: discounting will cut margin if the real cause is nearby construction or inventory mismatch
planSpec.requiredBeat: Chris replaces the blunt problem sales are down with branches for foot traffic, conversion, and basket size, then tests each before choosing an action.

examples.scenario: Chris needed three quiet Tuesdays to stop calling the symptom the problem. The daily sales ledger said weekday sales were down, but the construction notice outside the shop and category inventory report pointed in different directions. Before running discounts, Chris rebuilt the issue as foot traffic, conversion, and basket size. He tested each branch and found the traffic drop before choosing an action.
examples.whatToDo: Replace sales are down with branches for foot traffic, conversion, and basket size. Test each branch before using discounts.
examples.whyItMatters: Discounting cuts margin if traffic, not price, is the cause. A sharper problem definition protects the action from the wrong diagnosis.

examples.title: Marit Refuses the Staff-Failed Line

planSpec.domain: an emergency-management office reviewing slow storm-shelter openings
planSpec.stakes: residents could wait outside shelters again if staffing, keys, and alert protocols remain one vague issue
planSpec.requiredBeat: At 7:05 a.m., Marit refuses to write staff failed, divides the process into alert, access, staffing, and supply branches, and marks which branch lacks evidence.

examples.scenario: Marit pins a shelter-opening timeline beside the radio log in the emergency-management office. The key-control sheet is incomplete, and the supply checklist arrived after the storm. A draft line says staff failed. Before the council review, Marit has to pick between defending that blame line and dividing the process. She creates alert, access, staffing, and supply branches, then marks the supply branch as lacking evidence.
examples.whatToDo: Replace the blame line with process branches. Separate alert, access, staffing, and supply before assigning cause or action.
examples.whyItMatters: A vague failure label can punish the wrong group and leave the real readiness gap untouched. Branches show what still lacks proof.

examples.title: Akira Draws Branches Before Buying Tools

planSpec.domain: a game-studio producer diagnosing repeated build failures
planSpec.audience: software production teams separating causes from fixes
planSpec.stakes: the team may buy tooling when build failures stem from asset handoff rules
planSpec.requiredBeat: "The failed build is not the problem yet," Akira says, then draws branches for assets, code merges, tests, and release timing before assigning fixes.

examples.scenario: Akira points to the projected error screen and says, "The build log is evidence, not the problem," with the error screen projected behind him. The asset handoff board is full of late texture files, and the release calendar is already slipping. Engineering wants a new build tool by Friday. Akira faces a choice: approve the tool request now or map the field first. He separates assets, merges, tests, and release timing before assigning fixes.
examples.whatToDo: Hold the tooling decision until assets, code merges, tests, and release timing are separated. Assign fixes only after evidence gathers on a branch.
examples.whyItMatters: Build failures can come from process, code, assets, or timing. Buying tools too early turns one possible fix into the problem definition.

questions.prompt: An analyst sees a report that treats late buses as the problem and immediately recommends more vehicles before checking dispatch logs, traffic pinch points, or transfer timing. What question should come first?
choices: How many buses can the city afford?, while giving the page a cleaner surface without fixing the logic
What is the visible symptom, and what possible causes could produce it?
Which route has the angriest riders?
questions.explanation: Problem definition comes before action. Cost and complaints matter later, but they do not separate symptom from cause.

questions.prompt: A hospital cafeteria assumes uneaten meals mean patients dislike the menu. What should the team test before funding menu work?
choices: Whether the cafeteria logo feels modern enough.
Whether nurses mention food during rounds.
Delivery timing, tray temperature, dietary fit, and menu choice as separate branches.
questions.explanation: The symptom can have several causes. Branching timing, temperature, diet, and menu keeps the team from buying a preferred fix too early.

questions.prompt: A lab manager sees a replication fail three times, and the team jumps straight to retraining staff before checking reagent quality, sample prep, or timing records. What is the risk?
choices: The action may target technique before reagent quality or sample prep is diagnosed.
Staff may feel criticized by the wording.
The report may need more charts and cleaner tables.
questions.explanation: Retraining assumes a cause. A cause tree lets technique compete with reagent and sample-prep branches before action is chosen.

questions.prompt: A bookshop owner sees sales down and plans discounts. Construction outside has reduced foot traffic. What was misdefined?
choices: The symptom was treated as the whole problem.
The inventory report was too detailed.
The discount should have been larger.
questions.explanation: Sales down is the visible result, not a diagnosis. Foot traffic, conversion, and basket size should be separated before choosing discounts.

questions.prompt: A shelter-opening review begins with staff failed. The radio log, key-control sheet, and supply checklist are incomplete. What should the reviewer do?
choices: Keep the blame line because accountability matters.
Divide the process into branches and mark which ones lack evidence.
Remove all evidence gaps from the public report.
questions.explanation: The process needs structure before blame. Alert, access, staffing, and supply may explain different parts, and missing evidence should stay visible.

questions.prompt: A game studio wants a new build tool after repeated build failures. Asset handoffs are late and tests are unstable. Which move protects the inquiry?
choices: Approve the tool because build failures are technical.
Cancel the release date until morale improves.
Map assets, code merges, tests, and release timing before approving a fix.
questions.explanation: Tooling is only one possible action. Branching the causes prevents the visible failure from becoming a purchase order by default.

questions.prompt: A problem-solving outline has a crisp final recommendation, but the problem statement is vague and diagnosis is skipped. What is the main weakness?
choices: The recommendation should use more confident wording.
The outline needs more indentation and cleaner labels.
The final hierarchy rests on unstructured inquiry.
questions.explanation: A polished answer cannot compensate for weak problem definition and diagnosis. The process behind the structure has to carry weight.

questions.prompt: A team draws a logic tree with twenty tiny branches, no evidence beside any branch, and no decision about which causes to test before the Friday review. What is the likely misuse?
choices: The tree has become busywork instead of opening a useful cause field.
Narrow the problem definition first because twenty branches may signal a poorly bounded issue rather than a weak tool.
The problem must already be solved.
questions.explanation: A logic tree should structure inquiry, not multiply branches forever. It helps when it exposes plausible causes that can be tested.

questions.prompt: A manager writes proposed action as the first line of the problem statement while the symptom and possible causes remain vague. What quick test exposes the issue?
choices: Make the action line shorter and present it as a cleaner problem statement.
Write three separate lines: symptom, possible causes, proposed action.
Move the action into a larger font so the team sees the proposed fix first.
questions.explanation: Separating symptom, causes, and action reveals when the preferred fix has been smuggled into the problem definition.

reviewCards.front: What are the three jobs to separate in problem solving?
reviewCards.back: Define the problem, diagnose why it exists, then choose what to do. When those jobs blur, a recommendation can sound firm while resting on weak inquiry.

reviewCards.front: A visible symptom is being treated as the problem. What should you do?
reviewCards.back: Name it as a symptom, then branch possible causes before choosing action. The first visible trouble is often not the actual problem.

reviewCards.front: A team draws a logic tree before picking a fix. What should the tree prevent?
reviewCards.back: It opens the field of possible causes so one favorite explanation does not take over before evidence is tested.

reviewCards.front: Why can a polished recommendation still be weak?
reviewCards.back: It may rest on a poor problem statement or skipped diagnosis. Structure in the final report needs structure in the inquiry behind it.

reviewCards.front: How do you catch a proposed fix hiding inside a problem statement?
reviewCards.back: Write three lines: symptom, possible causes, proposed action. If the first line and third line match, the problem has not been defined cleanly.

implementationPlan.title: Structure the Inquiry First
implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to keep problem definition, diagnosis, and action separate. The skill is slowing down the first obvious fix long enough to branch causes and test the field.

ifThenPlans.plan: If the first sentence names a fix, then rewrite it as a symptom and list at least three possible causes.
If complaints point to one visible failure, then branch timing, quality, process, and user-fit causes before spending money.
If blame appears before evidence, then map the process stages and mark which branch each evidence item supports.
If a tool purchase is proposed after repeated failures, then separate asset, code, test, and timing causes before approving it.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: For one current issue, write three lines: symptom, possible causes, proposed action. If the first and third lines are the same, stop and define the problem again.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each week, choose one recommendation and trace the inquiry behind it. Verify that the problem, causes, and action are separate before improving the final wording.

memorableLines.text: Definition comes first. Diagnosis comes second. Action comes third.
memorableLines.why: It gives the process sequence in a form readers can retrieve.

memorableLines.text: A polished hierarchy cannot rescue a lazy inquiry.
memorableLines.why: It names the central failure sharply.

memorableLines.text: The final recommendation gains force because the process behind it has stopped bluffing.
memorableLines.why: It links process discipline to the credibility of the answer.
